title: Bread and Circuses
objective: After this level you can explain the grain dole and public games and why rulers provided them.
summary: Rome fed about 200,000 citizens with free grain and staged huge free games. A poet mocked it as “bread and circuses.”

cards.headline: A Roman poet said his people wanted only two things: bread and circuses.
cards.body: He wasn’t paying them a compliment. So what were the bread and the circuses, and who was handing them out?

cards.headline: Free grain
cards.body: The bread was real. Rome gave free grain to many citizens living in the city, and under Augustus about 200,000 people received it. That’s a lot of mouths to feed. Much of that grain came from Egypt, a province under the emperor’s personal control. The emperor didn’t just run the city. He ran its pantry.

cards.headline: Free games
cards.body: The circuses were real too. Public games, ludi, began as religious festivals and grew into huge free entertainments. Worship had become a show. Who paid? Emperors and politicians, who funded games and food to win popularity and keep the city calm. Crowd control, served with a side of spectacle.

cards.context: The poet Juvenal said the Roman people, who once handed out commands, now wanted only these two things. His jab: citizens who used to give the orders had settled for free food and shows.

cards.headline: Bread and circuses: explained
learned: Rome fed citizens with free grain

questions.prompt: About how many people received free grain under Augustus?
questions.explanation: Under Augustus about 200,000 people in Rome received free grain.

questions.prompt: Why did emperors pay for grain and games?

options.label: The law required it of every consul
To win popularity and keep the city calm
Because farmers refused to sell grain

questions.explanation: Feeding and entertaining the crowd kept rulers popular and the city calm.

questions.prompt: From Level 31: which reformer had pushed for cheap grain for citizens?
questions.explanation: Gaius Gracchus pushed wider reforms, including cheap grain, before he was killed in 121 BCE.
